summary: The United Kingdom is made up of England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland; it was once the world's largest colonial empire and is the birthplace of the Industrial Revolution and parliamentary democracy.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: Christianity reached Britain in Roman times, and in 597 the Pope sent Augustine to Canterbury to preach to the Anglo-Saxons. In 1534 Henry VIII broke with Rome over the question of his divorce and issued the Act of Supremacy, establishing the Church of England (Anglican Church), while in Scotland a Presbyterian reformation was driven by John Knox in 1560; in the 18th century Methodism, founded by John Wesley, spread widely among the working class. However, in the 2021 census the share of people in England and Wales identifying as Christian fell below half for the first time.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: After World War II British society secularized rapidly, church attendance kept falling, and the spread of education, urbanization and the welfare state reduced the role of religion in life. In the 2021 census about 37% of residents of England and Wales chose "no religion", a sharp rise from ten years earlier, and among the younger generation the non-religious have become a majority.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: The growth of Britain's Muslim population is closely tied to the history of the British Empire. During the postwar labor shortage of the 1950s–60s, large numbers of immigrants from Pakistan, Bangladesh (then East Pakistan) and India came to work in British textile mills and factories, concentrating in Birmingham, Bradford, Manchester and London's East End. Today British Muslims are mainly of South Asian origin, and there are also immigrants from Somalia, the Middle East and elsewhere.

ranking.name: Hinduism
ranking.description: Hindus are mainly from the Indian immigration of the 1950s–60s and from the tens of thousands of East African Indians expelled by Ugandan president Idi Amin in 1972, many of whom settled in Leicester and north-west London. The large Hindu temple opened in Neasden, London, in 1995 is one of the largest traditional Hindu temples outside India.

ranking.name: Sikhism
ranking.description: Most Sikhs come from Punjab in India; in the period of British India many Sikhs served in the British Army, and in the postwar immigration wave of the 1950s–60s they worked in factories in places such as Southall in London and Birmingham and built gurdwaras, making Britain one of the largest Sikh communities outside India.

religion.background: Britain was Christianized twice, in Roman times and in the 6th–7th centuries; the Reformation of Henry VIII in the 16th century established the Church of England with the monarch at its head, while Scotland developed a Presbyterian established church, and for the following centuries Catholics and nonconformists were subject to legal restrictions. The Evangelical revival and Methodism had a profound influence in the 18th–19th centuries. After World War II the British Empire dissolved, and immigrants from South Asia, the Caribbean and Africa brought Islam, Hinduism and Sikhism, while society secularized rapidly, producing today's pattern in which Christianity, no religion and a diversity of faiths coexist.

language.official: The United Kingdom has no statutory official language; English is the de facto national language, and Welsh has official status in Wales.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: English originated with the Germanic tribes, such as the Angles and Saxons, who migrated to Britain in the 5th century, and later absorbed the Old Norse of the Vikings; after the Norman Conquest of 1066, French became the language of the upper classes for three hundred years, adding a large French vocabulary to English. Caxton's introduction of printing in 1476 and Johnson's publication of A Dictionary of the English Language in 1755 promoted the standardization of written English. With the expansion of the British Empire English became a global lingua franca, and in Britain itself it is the mother tongue of the vast majority.

ranking.name: Polish
ranking.description: During World War II large numbers of Polish soldiers fought in Britain alongside the government-in-exile, and the Polish Resettlement Act of 1947 allowed about two hundred thousand to stay and settle. When Poland joined the EU in 2004, Britain immediately opened its labor market and hundreds of thousands of Poles moved in, and in the 2011 census Polish had become the second most common language in England. After the 2016 Brexit referendum, some Poles returned to their home country.

ranking.name: Welsh
ranking.description: Welsh belongs to the Brittonic branch of the Celtic languages and was used in Britain earlier than English. The Acts of Union of 1536 and 1543 required English for public office, and in the 19th century schools even punished pupils who spoke their mother tongue with the "Welsh Not", causing a sharp decline. A language movement arose from the 1960s, a Welsh-language television channel was established in 1982, and in 2011 Welsh became an official language of Wales; about one fifth of Welsh people now speak it.

language.history: In Roman times the inhabitants of Britain spoke Celtic languages; after the Anglo-Saxon invasion of the 5th century, Old English replaced Celtic in the south-east, and Celtic languages retreated to Wales, the Scottish Highlands, Cornwall and elsewhere. The conquests of the Vikings and the Normans brought a large vocabulary of Norse and French into English, and the "Great Vowel Shift" of the 15th–16th centuries formed the pronunciation of modern English. The Industrial Revolution and imperial expansion took English to the world; in the late 20th century preservation movements arose for Celtic languages such as Welsh and Scottish Gaelic, while immigrants brought languages such as Polish, Punjabi and Urdu.

ranking.name: Fish and chips
ranking.description: Cod or haddock coated in batter and deep-fried, served with thick-cut fried potato chips, sprinkled with malt vinegar and salt, often accompanied by mushy peas, and eaten takeaway wrapped in paper.
ranking.history: The method of frying fish in a coating is generally thought to have been brought in the 17th century by Sephardic Jews who had moved to Britain from Portugal and Spain, who fried fish before the Sabbath so that it could be eaten cold. Fried chips became popular in the north of England in the 19th century, and in the 1860s shops selling the two together appeared in London and Lancashire. During the Industrial Revolution it became a cheap and filling dinner for the working class, and during World War II the government deliberately did not ration it in order to maintain morale. Britain still has over ten thousand fish and chip shops, and it is the most representative national food.

ranking.name: Full English breakfast
ranking.description: A hearty breakfast plate of fried egg, bacon, sausage, baked beans, grilled tomato, mushrooms and toast, with black pudding added in some regions.
ranking.history: The tradition of the full breakfast can be traced to the country gentry of the Victorian era, who used a lavish breakfast to show wealth and hospitality. In the early 20th century this style of eating spread to the working class, becoming the "fry-up" that gave energy before work. Different versions developed in different places, for example haggis in Scotland and potato bread in Northern Ireland. Today it is the signature of British cafés and hotel breakfasts, and also the representative dish of weekend brunch.

ranking.name: Sunday roast
ranking.description: Roast beef, lamb or chicken as the main dish, served with roast potatoes, Yorkshire pudding, vegetables and gravy, and eaten at midday on Sunday.
ranking.history: The custom of the Sunday roast is linked to the British tradition of going to church on Sunday: people put the meat in the oven before leaving, and on returning from the service it was ready to eat. In the 18th century the British took pride in eating roast beef, and the song "The Roast Beef of Old England", written by the author Henry Fielding in 1731, became a patriotic symbol. Recipes for Yorkshire pudding appeared in cookbooks in the mid-18th century, originally used to catch the fat dripping from the roasting meat. To this day it remains an important ritual of weekend family gatherings in Britain.

ranking.name: Chicken tikka masala
ranking.description: Pieces of yogurt-and-spice-marinated grilled chicken placed in an orange-red thick sauce cooked from tomato, cream and spices, served with basmati rice or naan.
ranking.history: It is generally thought that this dish was born in Britain in the 1970s; a popular account says that a chef at an Indian restaurant in Glasgow, to satisfy British customers who asked for "gravy", added the grilled chicken pieces to a tomato soup sauce. Britain's "Indian restaurants" are mostly run by immigrants from the Sylhet region of Bangladesh, a microcosm of the postwar history of South Asian immigration. In 2001 Foreign Secretary Robin Cook called it "a true British national dish", symbolizing the multicultural character of British society.

ranking.name: Shepherd's pie
ranking.description: Minced lamb stewed with onion and carrot in gravy is spread in a baking dish, covered with a layer of mashed potato, and baked until the top is golden.
ranking.history: This type of pie originated in the late 18th century, when the potato became the cheap staple of the British poor; housewives chopped up the meat left over from the Sunday roast, covered it with mashed potato and baked it to avoid waste, at first calling it "cottage pie". From the 19th century the version made with lamb came to be called "shepherd's pie", connected with sheep farming in northern Britain and Scotland. It remains a classic home dish in British schools, pubs and homes.
